claim: Rickettsia parkeri elicits skin lesions (eschars) and disseminated disease in humans.
source: The tick-borne pathogen Rickettsia parkeri elicits skin lesions (eschars) and disseminated disease in humans; however, inbred mice are generally resistant to infection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on human R. parkeri disease.

claim: Inbred mice are generally resistant to Rickettsia parkeri infection.
source: The tick-borne pathogen Rickettsia parkeri elicits skin lesions (eschars) and disseminated disease in humans; however, inbred mice are generally resistant to infection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: Intradermal infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice with as few as 10 R. parkeri elicits eschar formation and disseminated, lethal disease.
source: We report that intradermal infection of mice lacking both interferon receptors (Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/-) with as few as 10 R. parkeri elicits eschar formation and disseminated, lethal disease.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing lesion formation and lethality at various doses including 10 bacteria.

claim: Eschars in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice exhibited necrosis and inflammation, with bacteria primarily found in leukocytes, similar to human infection.
source: Similar to human infection, eschars exhibited necrosis and inflammation, with bacteria primarily found in leukocytes.
evidence: This is supported by histological and immunohistochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The actin-based motility factor Sca2 is required for dissemination from the skin to internal organs.
source: Using this model, we find that the actin-based motility factor Sca2 is required for dissemination from the skin to internal organs, and the outer membrane protein OmpB contributes to eschar formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced bacterial burdens in spleens and livers after intradermal infection with sca2 mutant bacteria.

claim: The outer membrane protein OmpB contributes to eschar formation.
source: Using this model, we find that the actin-based motility factor Sca2 is required for dissemination from the skin to internal organs, and the outer membrane protein OmpB contributes to eschar formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing less severe skin lesions in mice infected with ompB mutant bacteria.

claim: Immunizing Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice with sca2 and ompB mutant R. parkeri protects against rechallenge.
source: Immunizing Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice with sca2 and ompB mutant R. parkeri protects against rechallenge, revealing live-attenuated vaccine candidates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing survival and reduced disease in immunized mice upon rechallenge.

claim: Discrepancies between mouse and human susceptibility to R. parkeri may be due to differences in interferon signaling.
source: Our results further suggest that discrepancies between mouse and human susceptibility may be due to differences in interferon signaling.
evidence: This is based on inference from the observation that interferon receptor-deficient mice develop disease similar to humans.

claim: Human disease caused by R. parkeri is characterized by a necrotic, dry skin lesion (eschar) at the infection site, as well as generalized rash, headache, fatigue, and fever.
source: Human disease caused by the tick-borne spotted fever group (SFG) pathogen Rickettsia parkeri is characterized by a necrotic, dry skin lesion (eschar) at the infection site, as well as generalized rash, headache, fatigue, and fever (Paddock et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature on human R. parkeri disease.

claim: There is no approved vaccine for R. parkeri or for the more virulent rickettsial pathogens.
source: There is no approved vaccine for R. parkeri or for the more virulent rickettsial pathogens that can cause fatal or latent disease (Osterloh, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: R. parkeri can be handled under biosafety level 2 (BSL2) conditions.
source: R. parkeri can be handled under biosafety level 2 (BSL2) conditions, and characterizing mouse models to recapitulate major features of human disease would enhance research efforts into understanding rickettsial pathogens and disease (Osterloh, 2017; Grasperge et al., 2012; Sunyakumthorn et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: R. parkeri is genetically similar to the more virulent human pathogens R. rickettsii and R. conorii.
source: R. parkeri is genetically similar to the more virulent human pathogens R. rickettsii and R. conorii (Roux and Raoult, 2000; Goddard, 2009), and it can be handled under BSL2 conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mutants of R. parkeri can be generated using transposon mutagenesis.
source: Moreover, mutants can be generated using transposon mutagenesis (Reed et al., 2014; Lamason et al., 2018), and small rodents including mice have been found as seropositive for R. parkeri in the wild (Moraru et al., 2013a; Moraru et al., 2013b; Krawczak et al., 2016; Barbieri et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Small rodents including mice have been found as seropositive for R. parkeri in the wild.
source: Moreover, mutants can be generated using transposon mutagenesis (Reed et al., 2014; Lamason et al., 2018), and small rodents including mice have been found as seropositive for R. parkeri in the wild (Moraru et al., 2013a; Moraru et al., 2013b; Krawczak et al., 2016; Barbieri et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inbred mice including C57BL/6 and BALB/c develop no or minor skin lesions upon intradermal infection with R. parkeri.
source: However, inbred mice including C57BL/6 and BALB/c develop no or minor skin lesions upon intradermal (i.d.) infection with R. parkeri (Grasperge et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A mouse model for R. parkeri that recapitulates eschar formation and dissemination via needle inoculation with low doses has remained elusive.
source: However, a model that recapitulates eschar formation and dissemination via needle inoculation with low doses of R. parkeri has remained elusive.
evidence: This is based on inference from prior literature and the need for the current study.

claim: Type I IFN (IFN-I) generally restricts viral replication, whereas IFN-γ generally restricts intracellular bacterial pathogens.
source: Type I IFN (IFN-I) generally restricts viral replication, whereas IFN-γ generally restricts intracellular bacterial pathogens (Raniga and Liang, 2018; Billiau and Matthys, 2009; Meunier and Broz, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Mice lacking either Ifnar1 or Ifngr1 are resistant to i.v. infection with R. parkeri, whereas double knockout Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice succumb.
source: We observed that mice lacking either gene encoding the receptors for IFN-I (Ifnar1) or IFN-γ (Ifngr1) are resistant to i.v. infection with R. parkeri, whereas double knockout (DKO) Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice succumb (Burke et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: IFNs redundantly protect against systemic R. parkeri.
source: This demonstrates that IFNs redundantly protect against systemic R. parkeri.
evidence: This is based on inference from the observation that single mutants are resistant but double mutants succumb.

claim: Actin-based motility is a virulence mechanism shared by divergent cytosolic bacterial pathogens including Rickettsia, Listeria, Burkholderia, Mycobacterium, and Shigella species.
source: One virulence mechanism shared by divergent cytosolic bacterial pathogens including Rickettsia, Listeria, Burkholderia, Mycobacterium, and Shigella species is the ability to undergo actin-based motility, which facilitates cell to cell spread (Choe and Welch, 2016; Lamason and Welch, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: R. parkeri actin-based motility occurs in two phases.
source: R. parkeri actin-based motility differs from that of other pathogens in that it occurs in two phases.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The first phase of R. parkeri actin-based motility requires the RickA protein, which elicits actin-based motility by activating the host Arp2/3 complex.
source: The first phase requires the RickA protein, which elicits actin-based motility by activating the host Arp2/3 complex (Gouin et al., 2004; Jeng et al., 2004); however, RickA is dispensable for cell to cell spread in vitro (Reed et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RickA is dispensable for cell to cell spread in vitro.
source: The first phase requires the RickA protein, which elicits actin-based motility by activating the host Arp2/3 complex (Gouin et al., 2004; Jeng et al., 2004); however, RickA is dispensable for cell to cell spread in vitro (Reed et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The second phase of R. parkeri actin-based motility requires the Sca2 protein.
source: The second phase requires the Sca2 protein (Reed et al., 2014; Kleba et al., 2010), which mimics eukaryotic formins to directly nucleate and elongate actin filaments (Reed et al., 2014; Haglund et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Sca2 mimics eukaryotic formins to directly nucleate and elongate actin filaments.
source: The second phase requires the Sca2 protein (Reed et al., 2014; Kleba et al., 2010), which mimics eukaryotic formins to directly nucleate and elongate actin filaments (Reed et al., 2014; Haglund et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Sca2 is required for efficient cell to cell spread.
source: Sca2 is required for efficient cell to cell spread, although it is not required for replication in epithelial cells or for avoiding antimicrobial autophagy (Reed et al., 2014; Kleba et al., 2010; Haglund et al., 2010; Engström et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Sca2 is not required for replication in epithelial cells or for avoiding antimicrobial autophagy.
source: Sca2 is required for efficient cell to cell spread, although it is not required for replication in epithelial cells or for avoiding antimicrobial autophagy (Reed et al., 2014; Kleba et al., 2010; Haglund et al., 2010; Engström et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: sca2 mutant R. rickettsii elicit reduced fever in guinea pigs when compared with wild-type R. rickettsii.
source: sca2 mutant R. rickettsii elicit reduced fever in guinea pigs when compared with wild-type (WT) R. rickettsii (Kleba et al., 2010), yet the explanation for reduced fever and the pathogenic role for Sca2 in vivo remains unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Sca2 is not essential for dissemination of R. parkeri within ticks.
source: Additionally, Sca2 is not essential for dissemination of R. parkeri within ticks (Harris et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The ability to avoid autophagy is a virulence strategy employed by intracellular pathogens, which for R. parkeri requires the abundant, conserved outer membrane protein B (OmpB).
source: A second virulence strategy employed by intracellular pathogens is the ability to avoid autophagy, which for R. parkeri requires the abundant, conserved outer membrane protein B (OmpB) (Engström et al., 2019; Engström et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ompB mutant R. parkeri are ubiquitylated and restricted by antimicrobial autophagy in mouse macrophages.
source: ompB mutant R. parkeri are ubiquitylated and restricted by antimicrobial autophagy in mouse macrophages, and OmpB is important for R. parkeri infection of internal organs in WT mice and for causing lethal disease in IFN receptor-deficient mice after i.v. infection (Burke et al., 2020; Engström et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: OmpB is important for R. parkeri infection of internal organs in WT mice and for causing lethal disease in IFN receptor-deficient mice after i.v. infection.
source: ompB mutant R. parkeri are ubiquitylated and restricted by antimicrobial autophagy in mouse macrophages, and OmpB is important for R. parkeri infection of internal organs in WT mice and for causing lethal disease in IFN receptor-deficient mice after i.v. infection (Burke et al., 2020; Engström et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: No or minor dermal lesions appeared at the site of infection in WT, single mutant Tlr4-/-, Ifnar1-/-, or Ifngr1-/- C57BL/6J mice or CD-1 mice after intradermal infection with 10^7 WT R. parkeri.
source: No or minor dermal lesions appeared at the site of infection in WT, single mutant Tlr4-/-, Ifnar1-/-, or Ifngr1-/- C57BL/6J mice or CD-1 mice (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and images shown in Figure 1.

claim: DKO Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- C57BL/6J mice developed delimited skin lesions measuring >1 cm in diameter that were necrotic, hardened, non-pruritic, and surrounded by an indurated red halo after intradermal infection with 10^7 WT R. parkeri.
source: In contrast, DKO Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- C57BL/6J mice developed delimited skin lesions measuring >1 cm in diameter that were necrotic, hardened, non-pruritic, and surrounded by an indurated red halo (Figure 1b), similar to human eschars (Figure 1c; Paddock et al., 2008; Paddock et al., 2004; Kaskas, 2014; Cragun et al., 2010; Herrick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and images shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Skin lesions in DKO Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice are similar to human eschars.
source: In contrast, DKO Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- C57BL/6J mice developed delimited skin lesions measuring >1 cm in diameter that were necrotic, hardened, non-pruritic, and surrounded by an indurated red halo (Figure 1b), similar to human eschars (Figure 1c; Paddock et al., 2008; Paddock et al., 2004; Kaskas, 2014; Cragun et al., 2010; Herrick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on comparison with human eschar images and citations to prior literature.

claim: In some cases, tails of DKO Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- or single mutant Ifngr1-/- mutant mice became inflamed after i.d. or i.v. infection.
source: In some cases, tails of DKO Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- or single mutant Ifngr1-/- mutant mice became inflamed after i.d. or i.v. infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Interferons redundantly control disease caused by R. parkeri in the skin.
source: These findings demonstrate that interferons redundantly control disease caused by R. parkeri in the skin and that i.d. infection of DKO Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice recapitulates the hallmark manifestation of human disease caused by R. parkeri.
evidence: This is based on inference from the observation that single mutants are resistant but double mutants develop disease.

claim: i.d. infection of DKO Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice recapitulates the hallmark manifestation of human disease caused by R. parkeri.
source: These findings demonstrate that interferons redundantly control disease caused by R. parkeri in the skin and that i.d. infection of DKO Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice recapitulates the hallmark manifestation of human disease caused by R. parkeri.
evidence: This is based on the observation of eschar-like lesions in infected mice.

claim: i.v. infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice with 10^7 R. parkeri elicits 100% lethality and 10^5 R. parkeri elicits no lethality.
source: Our previous observations using the i.v. route revealed dose-dependent lethality in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice, with 107 R. parkeri eliciting 100% lethality and 105 R. parkeri eliciting no lethality (Burke et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: R. parkeri are present in tick saliva at a concentration of approximately 10^4 per 1 μl, and approximately 10^7 R. parkeri are found in tick salivary glands.
source: R. parkeri are present in tick saliva at a concentration of approximately 104 per 1 μl, and approximately 107 R. parkeri are found in tick salivary glands (Suwanbongkot et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Skin lesion formation occurs at all infectious doses from 10^7 to 10 bacteria in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice after intradermal infection.
source: We observed skin lesion formation at all infectious doses, from 107 to 10 bacteria (Figure 1d), suggesting that i.d. infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice elicits lesions with doses similar to what is delivered by tick infestation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and images shown in Figure 1d.

claim: i.d. infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice elicits lesions with doses similar to what is delivered by tick infestation.
source: We observed skin lesion formation at all infectious doses, from 107 to 10 bacteria (Figure 1d), suggesting that i.d. infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice elicits lesions with doses similar to what is delivered by tick infestation.
evidence: This is based on inference from the observation of lesion formation at low doses and comparison with tick-delivered doses.

claim: Intradermally infected DKO Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice lost significant body weight when compared with WT mice.
source: Intradermally infected DKO Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/ mice lost significant body weight (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) and body temperature (Figure 2b; animals were euthanized when body temperature fell below 90°F / 32.2°C) when compared with WT mice, whereas infected single mutant Tlr4-/-, Ifnar1-/-, or Ifngr1-/- mice did not.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Intradermally infected DKO Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice lost significant body temperature when compared with WT mice.
source: Intradermally infected DKO Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/ mice lost significant body weight (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) and body temperature (Figure 2b; animals were euthanized when body temperature fell below 90°F / 32.2°C) when compared with WT mice, whereas infected single mutant Tlr4-/-, Ifnar1-/-, or Ifngr1-/- mice did not.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Infected single mutant Tlr4-/-, Ifnar1-/-, or Ifngr1-/- mice did not lose significant body weight or body temperature after intradermal infection with R. parkeri.
source: Intradermally infected DKO Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/ mice lost significant body weight (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) and body temperature (Figure 2b; animals were euthanized when body temperature fell below 90°F / 32.2°C) when compared with WT mice, whereas infected single mutant Tlr4-/-, Ifnar1-/-, or Ifngr1-/- mice did not.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and 2b.

claim: 10^7 bacteria elicited similar lesion responses as 10^5, 10^4, 10^3, and 10^2 bacteria in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice.
source: Whereas 107 bacteria elicited similar responses as 105, 104, 103, and 102 bacteria (Figure 2c), lesions were less severe when mice were infected with 101 bacteria compared with 107 bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Lesions were less severe when mice were infected with 10^1 bacteria compared with 10^7 bacteria.
source: Whereas 107 bacteria elicited similar responses as 105, 104, 103, and 102 bacteria (Figure 2c), lesions were less severe when mice were infected with 101 bacteria compared with 107 bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: If mice survived, lesions healed over the course of approximately 15–40 days post infection at all doses.
source: If mice survived, lesions healed over the course of approximately 15–40 days post infection (d.p.i.) at all doses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Upon i.d. delivery of 10^7 R. parkeri, 8 of 12 Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice exhibited lethargy, paralysis, or body temperatures below 90°F and were euthanized.
source: Upon i.d. delivery of 107 R. parkeri, 8 of 12 Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice exhibited lethargy, paralysis, or body temperatures below 90oF, at which point they were euthanized, whereas delivery of the same dose of bacteria to WT and single mutant mice did not elicit lesions and all survived (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Delivery of 10^7 R. parkeri to WT and single mutant mice did not elicit lesions and all survived.
source: Upon i.d. delivery of 107 R. parkeri, 8 of 12 Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice exhibited lethargy, paralysis, or body temperatures below 90oF, at which point they were euthanized, whereas delivery of the same dose of bacteria to WT and single mutant mice did not elicit lesions and all survived (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Lower doses of R. parkeri elicited body weight loss, body temperature loss, and lethal disease in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice.
source: Lower doses of R. parkeri also elicited body weight loss (Figure 2a), body temperature loss (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and lethal disease (Figure 2d) in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a, 2d, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Degrees of lethality between different doses in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice were not significantly different from one another.
source: Degrees of lethality between different doses in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice were not significantly different from one another, and the cause of lethality in this model remains unclear.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of survival data.

claim: i.d. infection can cause lethal disease in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice with ~10,000-fold lower dose of bacteria than i.v. infection.
source: Nevertheless, these findings reveal that i.d. infection can cause lethal disease in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice with ~10,000-fold lower dose of bacteria than i.v. infection.
evidence: This is based on comparison of doses required for lethality via different routes.

claim: Bacteria were not recoverable from spleens and livers of intradermally infected WT mice at 5 d.p.i.
source: Bacteria were not recoverable from spleens and livers of intradermally infected WT mice, suggesting that they did not disseminate from the skin to internal organs in high numbers (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Bacteria were recovered from spleens and livers of intradermally infected Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice at 5 d.p.i.
source: In contrast, bacteria were recovered from spleens and livers of intradermally infected Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice at 5 d.p.i. (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: i.d. infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice with R. parkeri causes systemic infection.
source: This demonstrates that i.d. infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice with R. parkeri causes systemic infection and can be used as a model for dissemination from the skin to internal organs.
evidence: This is based on inference from the recovery of bacteria from internal organs.

claim: WT mice infected i.d. with 10^3 R. parkeri exhibited no discernible inflammation in the skin at 4, 7, or 12 d.p.i.
source: WT mice infected i.d. with 103 R. parkeri exhibited no discernible inflammation in the skin at 4, 7, or 12 d.p.i. (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: At 4 d.p.i., Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice infected with 10^3 R. parkeri exhibited mild inflammation characterized by dermal inflammatory foci composed of neutrophils and macrophages, with high numbers of intralesional rickettsiae.
source: In contrast, at 4 d.p.i., Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice infected with 103 R. parkeri exhibited mild inflammation characterized by dermal inflammatory foci composed of neutrophils and macrophages, with high numbers of intralesional rickettsiae (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by histological and immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: By 7 d.p.i., the inflammation throughout the skin of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice was severe, with large coalescing foci of predominantly neutrophils and fewer macrophages within areas of fibrosis, associated with abundant rickettsiae.
source: By 7 d.p.i., the inflammation throughout the skin was severe, with large coalescing foci of predominantly neutrophils and fewer macrophages within areas of fibrosis, associated with abundant rickettsiae.
evidence: This is supported by histological observations.

claim: The epidermis of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice had multifocal coagulative necrosis associated with fibrin thrombosis of the underlying dermal capillaries at 7 d.p.i.
source: The epidermis had multifocal coagulative necrosis associated with fibrin thrombosis of the underlying dermal capillaries (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The inflammation in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice was still severe and associated with large numbers of intralesional rickettsiae at 12 d.p.i., accompanied by extensive coagulative necrosis of the skin.
source: The inflammation was still severe and associated with large numbers of intralesional rickettsiae at 12 d.p.i., accompanied by extensive coagulative necrosis of the skin (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: R. parkeri causes extensive necrosis and inflammatory cell infiltration of the skin of i.d.-infected Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice, with primary staining within neutrophils and macrophages.
source: Together, this indicates that R. parkeri causes extensive necrosis and inflammatory cell infiltration of the skin of i.d.-infected Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice, with primary staining within neutrophils and macrophages.
evidence: This is based on inference from histological and immunohistochemical observations.

claim: In the lungs of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice, inflammatory foci were scattered throughout the parenchyma, with several cells morphologically compatible with neutrophils containing rickettsiae.
source: In the lungs of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice, inflammatory foci were scattered throughout the parenchyma, with several cells morphologically compatible with neutrophils containing rickettsiae (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Rickettsiae were evident in some cells lining small vessels in the lungs, interpreted as endothelial cells.
source: In one tissue section, rickettsiae were also evident in some cells lining small vessels and therefore interpreted as endothelial cells.
evidence: This is based on histological observation and interpretation.

claim: Rickettsial immunostaining was not observed in the brain after i.d. infection with 10^3 R. parkeri.
source: In the brain, rickettsial immunostaining was not observed after i.d. infection with 103 R. parkeri, but infection with a higher dose (106) resulted in low number of rickettsial bacteria in the leptomeninges and the choroid plexus, in regions moderately infiltrated by neutrophils and macrophages (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claim: Infection with 10^6 R. parkeri resulted in low number of rickettsial bacteria in the leptomeninges and the choroid plexus of the brain, in regions moderately infiltrated by neutrophils and macrophages.
source: In the brain, rickettsial immunostaining was not observed after i.d. infection with 103 R. parkeri, but infection with a higher dose (106) resulted in low number of rickettsial bacteria in the leptomeninges and the choroid plexus, in regions moderately infiltrated by neutrophils and macrophages (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: R. parkeri disseminates from the skin to internal organs, where they are primarily found in macrophages and neutrophils.
source: These data demonstrate that R. parkeri disseminates from the skin to internal organs, where they are again primarily found in macrophages and neutrophils.
evidence: This is based on inference from immunohistochemical observations in multiple organs.

claim: In WT mice after i.v. infection, little to no inflammation or lesions were observed in spleens and livers.
source: In WT mice, we observed little to no inflammation or lesions.
evidence: This is supported by histological observations.

claim: Both spleens and livers of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice after i.v. infection had fibrinoid vascular wall degeneration, endothelial hypertrophy, fibrin thrombi in medium caliber vessels, and marked inflammation composed predominantly of macrophages.
source: In contrast, both organs of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice had fibrinoid vascular wall degeneration, endothelial hypertrophy, fibrin thrombi in medium caliber vessels, and marked inflammation that was composed predominantly of macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by histological observations.

claim: In WT mice after i.v. infection, rickettsiae were infrequent and were found in macrophages in the red pulp of the spleen and scarcely throughout the liver in Kupffer cells.
source: In WT mice, rickettsiae were infrequent and were found in macrophages in the red pulp of the spleen and scarcely throughout the liver in Kupffer cells (Figure 3g,h; Bonell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3g and 3h.

claim: In Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice after i.v. infection, rickettsiae were abundant in the splenic red pulp, primarily infecting histiocytes/macrophages.
source: In contrast, in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice, rickettsiae were abundant in the splenic red pulp, primarily infecting histiocytes/macrophages (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: In the liver of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice after i.v. infection, rickettsiae were abundant in macrophages within the granulomas.
source: In the liver of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice, rickettsiae were abundant in macrophages within the granulomas (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3h.

claim: No immunostaining for Rickettsia was observed in endothelial cells or vessels in the spleen or liver after i.v. infection.
source: We did not observe any immunostaining for Rickettsia in endothelial cells or vessels in the spleen or liver after i.v. infection.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical observations.

claim: Macrophages are the primary cell type affected by R. parkeri in the spleen and liver after i.v. infection.
source: Together, these findings reveal that macrophages are the primary cell type affected by R. parkeri in the spleen and liver after i.v. infection.
evidence: This is based on inference from immunohistochemical observations.

claim: Upon i.v. infection with 5 × 10^6 bacteria, sca2::Tn mutant R. parkeri caused reduced lethality compared to WT bacteria in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice.
source: Upon i.v. infection with 5 × 106 bacteria (Figure 4) or 107 bacteria (Figure 4b), we observed that sca2::Tn mutant R. parkeri caused reduced lethality compared to WT bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4a and 4b.

claim: i.d. infection with sca2::Tn mutant bacteria elicited significantly less lethality and weight loss as compared to WT bacteria.
source: Similarly, i.d. infection with sca2::Tn mutant bacteria elicited significantly less lethality (Figure 4c) and weight loss (Figure 4d) as compared to WT bacteria and no severe temperature loss (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by survival and weight data shown in Figure 4c and 4d.

claim: I.v. infection with MC1_RS08740::Tn R. parkeri caused lethality to a similar degree as WT R. parkeri.
source: I.v. infection with MC1_RS08740::Tn R. parkeri caused lethality to a similar degree as WT R. parkeri (Figure 4a), demonstrating that the transposon likely does not significantly impact R. parkeri fitness in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The transposon likely does not significantly impact R. parkeri fitness in vivo.
source: I.v. infection with MC1_RS08740::Tn R. parkeri caused lethality to a similar degree as WT R. parkeri (Figure 4a), demonstrating that the transposon likely does not significantly impact R. parkeri fitness in vivo.
evidence: This is based on inference from the observation that a control transposon mutant behaves like WT.

claim: The actin-based motility factor Sca2 is required for causing lethal disease in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the actin-based motility factor Sca2 is required for causing lethal disease in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice.
evidence: This is based on inference from the observation that sca2 mutant bacteria cause reduced lethality.

claim: Upon i.d. inoculation, Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice infected with sca2::Tn mutant bacteria developed skin lesions that were of similar severity to lesions caused by WT R. parkeri.
source: Unexpectedly, upon i.d. inoculation, Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice infected with sca2::Tn mutant bacteria developed skin lesions that were of similar severity to lesions caused by WT R. parkeri; however, the lesions elicited by sca2 mutant bacteria appeared significantly earlier than lesions caused by WT bacteria (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by lesion scoring data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Lesions elicited by sca2 mutant bacteria appeared significantly earlier than lesions caused by WT bacteria.
source: Unexpectedly, upon i.d. inoculation, Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice infected with sca2::Tn mutant bacteria developed skin lesions that were of similar severity to lesions caused by WT R. parkeri; however, the lesions elicited by sca2 mutant bacteria appeared significantly earlier than lesions caused by WT bacteria (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by lesion scoring data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Actin-based motility may enable R. parkeri to avoid a rapid onset of inflammation in the skin.
source: Further examinations will be required to better evaluate this observation; however, it may suggest that actin-based motility enables R. parkeri to avoid a rapid onset of inflammation in the skin.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observation of earlier lesion appearance with sca2 mutant bacteria.

claim: No significant differences in vascular damage were observed when comparing WT and sca2::Tn R. parkeri infections in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice using an infectious dose of 10^7 R. parkeri.
source: No significant differences were observed when comparing WT and sca2::Tn R. parkeri infections in Ifnar1-/-Ifngr1-/- mice using an infectious dose of 107 R. parkeri in the larger surrounding area (Figure 4g) or at the site of infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence data shown in Figure 4g and Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Significantly more fluorescence was observed in the skin of infected Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice as compared to WT mice.
source: However, significantly more fluorescence was observed in the skin of infected Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice as compared to WT mice (Figure 4g), demonstrating that interferons protect against increased vascular permeability during R. parkeri infection.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Interferons protect against increased vascular permeability during R. parkeri infection.
source: However, significantly more fluorescence was observed in the skin of infected Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice as compared to WT mice (Figure 4g), demonstrating that interferons protect against increased vascular permeability during R. parkeri infection.
evidence: This is based on inference from the fluorescence assay data.

claim: Sca2 likely does not significantly enhance R. parkeri spread throughout the skin during i.d. infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice.
source: Together, the gross pathological analysis and fluorescence-based assay suggest that Sca2 likely does not significantly enhance R. parkeri spread throughout the skin during i.d. infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice.
evidence: This is based on inference from lesion scoring and fluorescence data.

claim: ActA enables L. monocytogenes to spread from cell to cell, escape antimicrobial autophagy, proliferate in mouse organs after i.v. infection, and cause lethal disease in mice.
source: ActA enables L. monocytogenes to spread from cell to cell (Choe and Welch, 2016; Lamason and Welch, 2017), escape antimicrobial autophagy (Cheng et al., 2018; Mitchell et al., 2018; Yoshikawa et al., 2009b; Yoshikawa et al., 2009a), proliferate in mouse organs after i.v. infection (Auerbuch et al., 2001; Le Monnier et al., 2007), and cause lethal disease in mice (Goossens et al., 1992; Brundage et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: ActA is required for bacterial survival in spleens and livers upon i.v. delivery.
source: We initially hypothesized that R. parkeri Sca2 plays a similar pathogenic role in vivo to ActA, which we found is required for bacterial survival in spleens and livers upon i.v. delivery (Figure 4h), in agreement with previous experiments (Auerbuch et al., 2001; Le Monnier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4h and citations to prior literature.

claim: Similar amounts of WT and sca2::Tn bacteria were recovered in spleens upon i.v. infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice.
source: However, when we examined bacterial burdens upon i.v. infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice with R. parkeri, similar amounts of WT and sca2::Tn bacteria were recovered in spleens (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial burden data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Significantly more sca2::Tn than WT R. parkeri were recovered in livers upon i.v. infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice.
source: We were also surprised to find that significantly more sca2::Tn than WT R. parkeri were recovered in livers (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial burden data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Sca2 is likely not essential for R. parkeri survival in blood, invasion of host cells, or intracellular survival in spleens and livers.
source: Nevertheless, these data reveal that Sca2 is likely not essential for R. parkeri survival in blood, invasion of host cells, or intracellular survival in spleens and livers.
evidence: This is based on inference from the observation that sca2 mutant bacteria are recovered from organs after i.v. infection.

claim: After i.d. infection, sca2::Tn mutant bacteria were ~20-fold reduced in their abundance in spleens and ~2-fold reduced in their abundance in livers as compared to WT R. parkeri.
source: After i.d. infection, sca2::Tn mutant bacteria were ~20-fold reduced in their abundance in spleens and ~2-fold reduced in their abundance in livers as compared to WT R. parkeri (Figure 4j).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial burden data shown in Figure 4j.

claim: Sca2 is required for R. parkeri dissemination from the skin to internal organs.
source: Together, these results suggest that Sca2 is required for R. parkeri dissemination from the skin to internal organs.
evidence: This is based on inference from the observation of reduced bacterial burdens in organs after i.d. infection with sca2 mutant bacteria.

claim: The sca2::Tn mutant grew similarly to WT bacteria in endothelial cells.
source: We found that the sca2::Tn mutant grew similarly to WT bacteria in endothelial cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a), consistent with previous reports in epithelial cells (Reed et al., 2014; Kleba et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro growth data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3a and citations to prior literature.

claim: No significant difference in bacterial survival was observed between WT and sca2::Tn bacteria in BMDMs in the presence or absence of IFN-β.
source: However, no significant difference in bacterial survival was observed between WT and sca2::Tn bacteria in BMDMs in the presence or absence of IFN-β (Figure 4—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro growth data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3b.

claim: WT and sca2 mutant R. parkeri elicited similar amounts of host cell death.
source: WT and sca2 mutant R. parkeri also elicited similar amounts of host cell death (Figure 4—figure supplement 3c) and IFN-I production (Figure 4—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This is supported by LDH release data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3c.

claim: WT and sca2 mutant R. parkeri elicited similar amounts of IFN-I production.
source: WT and sca2 mutant R. parkeri also elicited similar amounts of host cell death (Figure 4—figure supplement 3c) and IFN-I production (Figure 4—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This is supported by IFN-I measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3d.

claim: The anti-rickettsial factor GBP2 localized to the surface of sca2::Tn mutant R. parkeri at similar frequency as with WT bacteria in the presence or absence of IFN-β.
source: Moreover, we found that the anti-rickettsial factor GBP2 localized to the surface of sca2::Tn mutant R. parkeri at similar frequency as with WT bacteria in the presence or absence of IFN-β (Figure 4—figure supplement 3e,f).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3e and 3f.

claim: Sca2 does not significantly enhance the ability of R. parkeri to evade interferon-stimulated antimicrobial genes or inflammasomes in vitro.
source: Together, these data suggest that Sca2 does not significantly enhance the ability of R. parkeri to evade interferon-stimulated antimicrobial genes or inflammasomes in vitro.
evidence: This is based on inference from multiple in vitro assays showing no difference between WT and sca2 mutant bacteria.

claim: ompB::TnSTOP R. parkeri harbors both a transposon and a stop codon in ompB but no other mutations as determined by whole genome sequencing.
source: We therefore investigated i.d. infection with ompB::TnSTOP R. parkeri, which harbors both a transposon and a stop codon in ompB but no other mutations as determined by whole genome sequencing (Engström et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work characterizing this mutant.

claim: ompB mutant R. parkeri are severely attenuated in mice, as evaluated by measuring p.f.u. in organs of WT mice after i.v. infection or by measuring lethality in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice after i.v. infection.
source: ompB mutant R. parkeri are severely attenuated in mice, as evaluated by measuring p.f.u. in organs of WT mice after i.v. infection (Engström et al., 2019) or by measuring lethality in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice after i.v. infection (Burke et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: i.d. infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice with ompB::TnSTOP R. parkeri caused no lethality or weight loss.
source: In contrast with WT bacteria, i.d. infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice with ompB::TnSTOP R. parkeri caused no lethality (Figure 5a) or weight loss (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by survival and weight data shown in Figure 5a and 5b.

claim: The ompB::TnSTOP mutant R. parkeri caused significantly less severe skin lesions than WT bacteria.
source: The ompB::TnSTOP mutant R. parkeri also caused significantly less severe skin lesions than WT bacteria (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by lesion scoring data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice can be used as a model to identify bacterial genes important for eschar formation.
source: These findings suggest that Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice can be used as a model to identify bacterial genes important for eschar formation.
evidence: This is based on inference from the observation that ompB mutant bacteria cause less severe lesions.

claim: All mice immunized with sca2 or ompB mutant R. parkeri survived i.v. rechallenge with 10^7 WT R. parkeri, whereas all naïve mice succumbed by 6 d.p.i.
source: All mice immunized with sca2 or ompB mutant R. parkeri survived, whereas all naïve mice succumbed to i.v. challenge by 6 d.p.i. (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Upon i.v. rechallenge, mice immunized with ompB and sca2 mutants did not lose significant weight or body temperature.
source: Upon i.v. rechallenge, mice immunized with ompB and sca2 mutants also did not lose significant weight (Figure 6b) or body temperature (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by weight and temperature data shown in Figure 6b and 6c.

claim: Mice immunized with ompB or sca2 mutant R. parkeri by i.d. infection or with sca2 mutant R. parkeri by i.v infection were protected from lethal disease upon i.d. rechallenge with 10^5 WT bacteria.
source: Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice were immunized with ompB or sca2 mutant R. parkeri by i.d. infection or with sca2 mutant R. parkeri by i.v infection and rechallenged 40 d later by i.d. infection with 105 WT bacteria. Immunized mice were protected from lethal disease (Figure 6d) and had less severe skin lesions than naïve mice (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Immunized mice had less severe skin lesions than naïve mice upon i.d. rechallenge.
source: Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice were immunized with ompB or sca2 mutant R. parkeri by i.d. infection or with sca2 mutant R. parkeri by i.v infection and rechallenged 40 d later by i.d. infection with 105 WT bacteria. Immunized mice were protected from lethal disease (Figure 6d) and had less severe skin lesions than naïve mice (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is supported by lesion scoring data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Attenuated R. parkeri mutants elicit robust protective immune responses.
source: These data indicate that attenuated R. parkeri mutants elicit robust protective immune responses, and that Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice may serve as tools to develop live attenuated R. parkeri vaccine candidates.
evidence: This is based on inference from the immunization and rechallenge data.

claim: Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice may serve as tools to develop live attenuated R. parkeri vaccine candidates.
source: These data indicate that attenuated R. parkeri mutants elicit robust protective immune responses, and that Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice may serve as tools to develop live attenuated R. parkeri vaccine candidates.
evidence: This is based on inference from the successful immunization experiments.

claim: IFN-I and IFN-γ redundantly protect inbred mice from eschar-associated rickettsiosis and disseminated disease by R. parkeri.
source: In this study, we find that IFN-I and IFN-γ redundantly protect inbred mice from eschar-associated rickettsiosis and disseminated disease by R. parkeri.
evidence: This is based on the observation that single mutants are resistant but double mutants develop disease.

claim: The striking difference between human and mouse susceptibilities to R. parkeri may be due to IFN signaling in the skin.
source: Eschar formation is a hallmark clinical feature of human disease caused by R. parkeri (Paddock et al., 2008; Paddock et al., 2004), and thus these findings suggest that the striking difference between human and mouse susceptibilities to R. parkeri may be due to IFN signaling in the skin.
evidence: This is based on inference from the observation that interferon receptor-deficient mice develop eschars similar to humans.

claim: R. parkeri Sca2 plays a role in dissemination.
source: Using this mouse model, we uncover a role for R. parkeri Sca2 in dissemination, for OmpB in skin lesion formation, and for both proteins in causing lethal disease.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced dissemination with sca2 mutant bacteria.

claim: R. parkeri OmpB plays a role in skin lesion formation.
source: Using this mouse model, we uncover a role for R. parkeri Sca2 in dissemination, for OmpB in skin lesion formation, and for both proteins in causing lethal disease.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing less severe lesions with ompB mutant bacteria.

claim: Both Sca2 and OmpB play a role in causing lethal disease.
source: Using this mouse model, we uncover a role for R. parkeri Sca2 in dissemination, for OmpB in skin lesion formation, and for both proteins in causing lethal disease.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced lethality with sca2 and ompB mutant bacteria.

claim: The IFN response in humans may be less well adapted to control R. parkeri than that in mice.
source: Importantly, the gross similarities we observe between human eschars (Paddock et al., 2008; Herrick et al., 2016) and skin lesions in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice may indicate that the IFN response in humans is less well adapted to control R. parkeri than that in mice.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observation that interferon-deficient mice develop disease similar to humans.

claim: Cytokine profiling and mRNA transcript analysis of human rickettsial infections reveals IFN-I and IFN-γ activation.
source: Cytokine profiling and mRNA transcript analysis of human rickettsial infections reveals IFN-I and IFN-γ activation (Cillari et al., 1996; Jia et al., 2020; de Sousa et al., 2007); however, it remains unclear whether human interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) are as protective as mouse ISGs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Human eschars resulting from R. parkeri infection are characterized by necrosis of the epidermis, vasculitis of small- to medium-sized dermal vessels, fibrin thrombi, infiltration by macrophages and neutrophils, and infection of macrophage/mononuclear cells.
source: Human eschars resulting from R. parkeri infection are characterized by necrosis of the epidermis, vasculitis of small- to medium-sized dermal vessels, fibrin thrombi, infiltration by macrophages and neutrophils, and infection of macrophage/mononuclear cells (Paddock et al., 2008; Herrick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on human pathology.

claim: Eschars elicited by R. parkeri in non-human primates revealed similar histological findings to human eschars and also bacteria within macrophages and neutrophils.
source: Eschars elicited by R. parkeri in non-human primates revealed similar histological findings and also bacteria within macrophages and neutrophils (Banajee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Similar histological findings were noted in guinea pigs after intraperitoneal infection with R. parkeri, as well as infection of mononuclear cells.
source: Similar histological findings were noted in guinea pigs after intraperitoneal infection with R. parkeri, as well as infection of mononuclear cells (Paddock et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: R. parkeri primary targeting of macrophages and neutrophils differs from cell types infected by R. rickettsii, which primarily targets endothelial cells.
source: We note that R. parkeri primary targeting of macrophages and neutrophils differs from cell types infected by R. rickettsii, which primarily targets endothelial cells (Walker and Ismail, 2008), and therefore infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice with R. parkeri is likely not an appropriate model for lethal Rocky Mountain spotted fever disease.
evidence: This is based on comparison with prior literature on R. rickettsii.

claim: Infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice with R. parkeri is likely not an appropriate model for lethal Rocky Mountain spotted fever disease.
source: We note that R. parkeri primary targeting of macrophages and neutrophils differs from cell types infected by R. rickettsii, which primarily targets endothelial cells (Walker and Ismail, 2008), and therefore infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice with R. parkeri is likely not an appropriate model for lethal Rocky Mountain spotted fever disease.
evidence: This is based on inference from the different cell tropisms of R. parkeri and R. rickettsii.

claim: The pathogen is numerous throughout the skin of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice, but their numbers are fewer in reported human eschar biopsies.
source: One contrasting finding in eschars of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice as compared to humans is the number of bacteria observed - we find that the pathogen is numerous throughout the skin of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice, but their numbers are fewer in reported human eschar biopsies (Paddock et al., 2008; Herrick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on comparison of histological observations with prior literature.

claim: Interferon receptor-deficient mice may be useful tools for modeling eschar-associated rickettsiosis at the cellular level.
source: Nevertheless, our pathological findings of infected interferon-receptor deficient mice are similar in many ways to the previous findings in humans, primates, and mice. Our results suggest that interferon receptor-deficient mice may be useful tools for modeling eschar-associated rickettsiosis at the cellular level.
evidence: This is based on inference from the similarities in pathology between mice and humans.

claim: O. tsutsugamushi elicits eschar formation in humans, but inbred mice do not recapitulate eschar formation during O. tsutsugamushi infection.
source: O. tsutsugamushi elicits eschar formation in humans, but inbred mice do not recapitulate eschar formation during O. tsutsugamushi infection (Sunyakumthorn et al., 2013), similar to R. parkeri.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: B. burgdorferi causes a skin rash at the site of tick bite as a hallmark feature of Lyme disease.
source: A second example may be Borrelia burgdorferi, a tick-borne pathogen that causes a skin rash at the site of tick bite as a hallmark feature of Lyme disease (Bratton et al., 2008), the most prevalent tick-borne disease in the United States (Bratton et al., 2008; Schwartz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Existing mouse models do not recapitulate skin rash formation following B. burgdorferi infection.
source: Existing mouse models also do not recapitulate skin rash formation following B. burgdorferi infection (Barthold et al., 1990; Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Other rickettsial pathogens including R. conorii, R. typhi, and R. akari cause no or limited disease in WT C57BL/6 mice.
source: Lastly, other rickettsial pathogens including R. conorii, R. typhi, and R. akari cause no or limited disease in WT C57BL/6 mice (Osterloh, 2017; Anderson and Osterman, 1980; Eisemann et al., 1984; Osterloh et al., 2016) and it remains unclear if interferons redundantly protect mice from these pathogens.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: i.d. infection can cause lethal disease with as few as 10 bacteria, ~ 10,000 fewer bacteria than i.v. infection.
source: Our observation that i.d. infection can cause lethal disease with as few as 10 bacteria, ~ 10,000 fewer bacteria than i.v. infection (Burke et al., 2020), suggests that R. parkeri may be highly adapted to reside in the skin.
evidence: This is based on comparison of doses required for lethality via different routes.

claim: R. parkeri may be highly adapted to reside in the skin.
source: Our observation that i.d. infection can cause lethal disease with as few as 10 bacteria, ~ 10,000 fewer bacteria than i.v. infection (Burke et al., 2020), suggests that R. parkeri may be highly adapted to reside in the skin.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the low dose required for disease via intradermal infection.

claim: Saliva from ticks, mosquitos, and sand flies enhances pathogenesis of arthropod-borne bacterial, viral, and parasitic pathogens.
source: Saliva from ticks, mosquitos, and sand flies enhances pathogenesis of arthropod-borne bacterial, viral, and parasitic pathogens (Pingen et al., 2017; Lestinova et al., 2017; Šimo et al., 2017), and non-human primates inoculated with R. parkeri exhibit altered inflammatory responses when administered after tick-bite (Banajee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Non-human primates inoculated with R. parkeri exhibit altered inflammatory responses when administered after tick-bite.
source: Saliva from ticks, mosquitos, and sand flies enhances pathogenesis of arthropod-borne bacterial, viral, and parasitic pathogens (Pingen et al., 2017; Lestinova et al., 2017; Šimo et al., 2017), and non-human primates inoculated with R. parkeri exhibit altered inflammatory responses when administered after tick-bite (Banajee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: For L. monocytogenes, the actin-based motility factor ActA enables the pathogen to survive in vivo, as actA mutant bacteria are over 1,000-fold attenuated by measuring lethality and by enumerating bacteria in spleens and livers of mice after i.v. infection.
source: For L. monocytogenes, the actin-based motility factor ActA enables the pathogen to survive in vivo, as actA mutant bacteria are over 1,000-fold attenuated by measuring lethality (Goossens et al., 1992; Brundage et al., 1993) and by enumerating bacteria in spleens and livers of mice after i.v. infection (Auerbuch et al., 2001; Le Monnier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Sca2 is not required for intracellular survival in organs upon i.v. infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice, but rather, is required for dissemination from skin to internal organs and lethality upon i.d. infection.
source: We find that Sca2 is not required for intracellular survival in organs upon i.v. infection of Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice, but rather, is required for dissemination from skin to internal organs and lethality upon i.d. infection.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing different roles for Sca2 depending on infection route.

claim: R. prowazekii and R. typhi encode a fragmented sca2 gene and undergo no or dramatically reduced frequency of actin-based motility, respectively.
source: R. prowazekii and R. typhi, which cause severe human disease, encode a fragmented sca2 gene (Ngwamidiba et al., 2005), and undergo no or dramatically reduced frequency of actin-based motility, respectively (Teysseire et al., 1992; Heinzen et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Sca2 is dispensable for R. parkeri dissemination in the tick vector.
source: Although it remains unclear why some Rickettsia species lost the ability to undergo actin-based motility, Sca2 is dispensable for R. parkeri dissemination in the tick vector (Harris et al., 2018), suggesting that actin-based motility may play a specific role in dissemination within mammalian hosts.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Actin-based motility may play a specific role in dissemination within mammalian hosts.
source: Although it remains unclear why some Rickettsia species lost the ability to undergo actin-based motility, Sca2 is dispensable for R. parkeri dissemination in the tick vector (Harris et al., 2018), suggesting that actin-based motility may play a specific role in dissemination within mammalian hosts.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observation that Sca2 is required for dissemination in mice but not in ticks.

claim: sca2 or ompB mutant R. parkeri elicit a robust protective immune response in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice.
source: We find that sca2 or ompB mutant R. parkeri elicit a robust protective immune response in Ifnar1-/-;Ifngr1-/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunization and rechallenge data.

claim: sca2 mutant R. rickettsii elicits antibody responses in guinea pigs.
source: These findings complement previous observations that sca2 mutant R. rickettsii elicits antibody responses in guinea pigs (Kleba et al., 2010), and expands upon these findings by demonstrating protection from rechallenge and revealing additional vaccine candidates.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: There are currently limited vaccine candidates that protect against rickettsial disease.
source: There are currently limited vaccine candidates that protect against rickettsial disease (Osterloh, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: R. parkeri resides directly in the host cytosol for days and could potentially be engineered to secrete foreign antigens for presentation by major histocompatibility complex I.
source: R. parkeri resides directly in the host cytosol for days and could potentially be engineered to secrete foreign antigens for presentation by major histocompatibility complex I.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential applications of R. parkeri as an antigen delivery platform.
